paras: The threatened lynching of Henry Hunt took place in January 1881, when crowds at Santa Ana and Los Angeles, California, threatened to hang Hunt, a prisoner charged with the fatal shooting of George W. Gillis at El Monte. Officers kept Hunt in custody, and he was later convicted and sentenced to life in prison. The episode reached papers across the country through an anecdote in which a speaker broke up the mob by proposing a collection for the dead officer's widow and orphans.

Gillis was shot at El Monte, near Los Angeles, on a Tuesday night in the week before January 14, 1881, and died of the wound. At Hunt's preliminary examination, the hotel keeper W. R. Dodson testified that Gillis broke up a fight between Hunt and a man named Tinker in his bar, declaring "I'm a peace officer," and that a shot followed as Hunt pushed him out the door. A Nevada telegraph item called the fugitive a desperado from Arizona, pursued by a large party, and added that if he were caught the county would "not be put to any expense."

According to a Los Angeles dispatch of January 14, a large crowd at Santa Ana made "loud threats" of lynching the night before, but officers slipped Hunt out a back door and brought him to Los Angeles. With rumors of a plan to take him from the authorities and hang him, the sheriff summoned a citizen posse to guard the jail, joined by the Los Angeles Guards. The same dispatch found the streets around the jail full of people but "little or no excitement."
A second dispatch that day reported that as Hunt was led back to jail from Justice Adams's office, a man holding a rope cried "Let us hang him" and was arrested by the sheriff.

A more dramatic account, printed by the Phoenix Herald on January 28 as having happened "a few days ago," had Col. Godfrey address "the surging mass" that wanted to lynch Hunt. A longer version credited to the Bangor Whig said a mob at the city prison cried "Lynch the scoundrel," that Sheriff Rowland called 200 leading citizens to his aid, and that the rioters surged against the prison with the hanging set for midnight. Just before midnight, in this telling, Col. Frank Godfrey proposed a collection for the murdered officer's widow and orphans, pledged $5 and named Joe Manning to pass the hat, and the mob dissolved.

Apart from the man with the rope, no arrests of anyone in the crowds appear in the coverage. Hunt's murder trial opened before Judge Sepulveda in mid-March 1881, and Hunt testified that he fired once at a man he believed was reaching for a pistol. He was sentenced to life in the State Prison and denied a new trial, and in November 1881 the Supreme Court affirmed the judgment.

The first reports were short Pacific Coast telegraph items in Nevada and Arizona papers that called Hunt "the assassin of Gillis" and "the murderer of Geo W. Gillis" before any trial. The Godfrey speech then traveled as a humorous item under headlines such as "How He Quelled a Mob" in Phoenix, "The Power of the Contribution Box" in Willimantic, Connecticut, and "Passing the Hat Among Lynchers" in Okolona, Mississippi. Copies in Portland, Maine, and New Haven credited the Bangor Whig, and the item still ran in March and April in Omaha and in Ottawa, Illinois.

Mississippi's Weekly Clarion headed its variant "A Shrewd Sheriff," while the South Kentuckian closed with the note that "the lynching was abandoned." These items made a joke of the mob's resolve rather than condemning or endorsing lynching, and none states Hunt's race or the crowd's.

The January 14 dispatch saw "little or no excitement" at the jail, while the anecdote described an implacable mob surging against the prison and the Weekly Clarion put it at "several thousand persons." The speaker is Col. Godfrey in the Phoenix Herald and Bangor Whig versions but an unnamed sheriff in the Weekly Clarion and South Kentuckian. The dispatches filed from Los Angeles on the day are closer to the events than the undated anecdote, which circulated mostly far from California.

bases: Crowds at Santa Ana and at the Los Angeles jail threatened to hang Hunt, a prisoner charged with murder, and officers guarded him; no one was killed (A2, A5, A12).
A crowd acting without authority threatened to hang Hunt for the alleged murder of an officer, but he stayed in custody, was tried and was sentenced to life, so no one was killed (A2, A12, A18).

Two independent January 14 Los Angeles dispatches report lynching cries and threats against the jailed Hunt (A2, A5), and the separately circulated Godfrey anecdote describes a mob at the prison (A7, A12), though its scale is disputed (A2).

framing.detail: A Nevada telegraph item reported the 'impression' that if Hunt were caught the county would be spared any expense, an allusion to lynching without comment.
Wire dispatches called Hunt 'the assassin of Gillis' and 'the murderer of Geo W. Gillis' and reported the guard on the jail.
The anecdote ran as a joke at the mob's expense under headlines like 'How He Quelled a Mob', 'A Shrewd Sheriff' and 'Passing the Hat Among Lynchers', neither condemning nor approving lynching.
